newsitem.title: UK: Key euro legal provisions delayed by UK election.
newsitem.headline: Key euro legal provisions delayed by UK election.

text.p: Legal provisions for the introduction of the euro after European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) have been delayed by the British election, a European Commission legal expert said on Wednesday.

William Harris-Burland, a principal admistrator at the commission, said regulations under Article 235 of the EC Treaty lay out the legal framework for converting the Ecu to the euro, as well as covering continuity of contracts and rounding rules.
They must be approved by all EU member states but Britain has the right to review them in parliament. The British election on May 1 has put any such review on ice, Harris-Burland said.
"Back rooms have to be prepared right from January 1999 to make conversion between the euro and existing currencies," Harris-Burland said at a conference on the legal implications of EMU in London.

The regulations, important for financial institutions designing bond issues, deals or contracts in force after 1999, were set to be adopted in the first quarter of this year after being approved at the Dublin EU finance ministers summit last year.

Cliff Dammers, secretary-general of the International Primary Market Association, said he expected Britain to hold up the process no matter who wins the election. The Labour Party will have other matters to deal with while the Conservative Party was obviously split on EMU.
"I am concerned that which ever party wins the election there will be further delays," he said. The delay will leave market players floundering.
Harris-Burland said the regulations would come into effect immediately after they are adopted by the EU Council and published in the Council's official journal.
He told the conference the second key legal issue for market players preparing for the euro were regulations under Article 109L(4) of the EC Treaty which cover monetary law.

The regulations allow for the substitution of the euro in place of national currencies, cover the transition period when old currencies trade alongside the euro, and issues relating to banknotes and coins.
Harris-Burland said the transition period will be extremely important for the euro.

"The approach is to have a legal big bang' but a practical transition period where for technical reason you keep the pfennig, the deutschemark, the French franc as a alternate unit," he said. "This will be the period when success or failure will manifest itself."

These regulations must be adopted by those members entering EMU and will come into force when the identity of participating countries becomes known, some time around May, 1998 Harris-Burland said. -- Jacqueline Thorpe, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
